title: Colorado AI Act and hiring: what employers must do from 2027
description: How Colorado's AI law affects hiring in 2027: SB 26-189 replaced the 2024 act, which hiring tools are covered, required notices, explanations, human review and records, and the draft rules.
short: Colorado's SB 26-189, effective January 1, 2027, replaces the 2024 Colorado AI Act. Employers using AI that materially influences hiring decisions must give notice, explain rejections within 30 days, allow data correction and human review, and keep records for three years.
body:
On January 1, 2027, Colorado's rules for automated hiring decisions take effect. They are not the rules most HR teams read about in 2024. In May 2026 the legislature passed SB 26-189, and Governor Polis signed it on May 14, 2026, replacing the original Colorado AI Act before it ever applied. According to Ogletree's summary of the new law, the duty of care, risk management program and impact assessment requirements are gone. In their place are notice, explanation, correction and human review duties that land directly on employers who use AI in hiring.

This explainer covers what changed, which hiring tools are in scope, what employers will have to do, and what the attorney general's draft rules add. It is a summary, not legal advice.

What the law covers

The law applies to covered automated decision making technology that materially influences a consequential decision. Employment is one of the decision areas, alongside education, housing, lending, insurance, health care and essential government services. Ogletree notes that the protected group includes employees, job applicants who live in Colorado and people evaluated for opportunities in the state, so an employer headquartered elsewhere can still be covered when it hires for Colorado roles.

"Materially influences" is the key test. A tool is in scope when its output is a non trivial factor that affects the outcome, for example by scoring, ranking or recommending candidates. Tools that only summarize, organize or display information for a person to review are treated differently, which matters for resume parsers and interview notetakers that do not score anyone. Our explainer on ATS and AI resume screening walks through which screening features rank and which only sort.

What employers will have to do

Based on the statute as summarized by Ogletree, an employer that uses a covered tool in hiring will need to:

  • Give candidates a notice before the tool is used.
  • Explain an adverse outcome, such as a rejection, within 30 days, including the role the technology played.
  • Let candidates correct inaccurate personal data used by the tool and, where commercially reasonable, request meaningful human review of the decision.
  • Keep records for at least three years.

Meaningful human review has a specific meaning. The reviewer must have authority to change the outcome, must consider the relevant evidence, must be trained, must not simply defer to the system's output and must understand the tool's intended use and limits. A recruiter who clicks approve on every AI shortlist does not meet that bar.

Vendors, staffing firms and contracts

Developers of covered tools must give deployers the documentation they need to meet these duties. Ogletree also reports that contract clauses that try to make one party indemnify the other for its own discrimination violations are void. In practice, employers should expect new vendor paperwork and should review indemnity terms in AI hiring contracts before renewal.

Using a staffing agency does not move the problem elsewhere. A National Law Review article from November 3, 2026 describes a draft rule example in which a staffing firm supplies an AI generated shortlist and the hiring employer is still responsible as the deployer.

The attorney general's draft rules

The Colorado attorney general is writing implementing rules. As Orrick explained on JD Supra, proposed rules were released in August 2026, an interim redline followed on October 6, and a rulemaking hearing was held on October 26. The drafts add detail that matters for recruiting teams:

  • A presumption that a tool materially influenced a decision when a person reviewed its score, ranking or recommendation and the final decision matched it. An employer can rebut the presumption by showing the output was a de minimis factor.
  • More specific adverse outcome explanations, including what the technology did.
  • Human reviewers can be internal staff or outside reviewers, as long as they can actually override the result.
  • Clear, plain language notices and an inventory of covered tools.

The rules were still in draft as of November 11, 2026, so details may change before January.

Enforcement

Only the attorney general can enforce the law; there is no private right of action. Ogletree reports a 60 day cure period for most violations, except knowing or repeated ones, and the National Law Review article describes the cure period as running until January 1, 2030. Existing discrimination claims under state and federal law remain available to candidates, so a biased tool is still a legal risk even when the new procedural duties are met.

A checklist for hiring teams

  1. List every tool that scores, ranks, filters or recommends candidates for Colorado roles.
  2. Ask each vendor for its developer documentation and how the tool reaches its output.
  3. Draft the pre use notice and an adverse outcome template that names the tool's role.
  4. Name and train human reviewers who can override results.
  5. Set up data correction requests and three year record retention.
  6. Review indemnity and allocation clauses in vendor and staffing contracts.

For how Colorado fits alongside New York City's audit rules and other regulation, read the guide chapter on bias, regulation and candidate rights, and for the screening tools most likely to be covered, see AI phone screening and AI interviewers.

faq.q: When does the Colorado AI Act apply to hiring?
faq.a: The replacement law, SB 26-189, takes effect on January 1, 2027. The original 2024 Colorado AI Act was repealed and replaced before it took effect.

faq.q: Does the Colorado AI law still require impact assessments?
faq.a: No. SB 26-189 removed the duty of care, risk management program and impact assessment requirements. It focuses on notice, adverse outcome explanations, data correction, human review and records.

faq.q: Which hiring tools are covered in Colorado?
faq.a: Tools that materially influence a hiring decision, for example by scoring, ranking or recommending candidates. Tools that only summarize or organize information for a person to review are treated differently.

faq.q: Can candidates sue under the Colorado AI law?
faq.a: No. The attorney general enforces it and there is no private right of action, but candidates can still bring discrimination claims under existing law.

faq.q: Is an employer responsible if a staffing agency uses the AI?
faq.a: Under the attorney general's draft rules, yes in the example described: when a staffing firm supplies an AI generated shortlist, the employer that relies on it is still responsible as the deployer.

title: EU AI Act and recruitment: what hiring teams must do, and when
description: How the EU AI Act applies to recruitment after the 2026 Digital Omnibus: which hiring tools are high risk, the new 2 December 2027 date, deployer duties, GDPR Article 22 and what to do now.
short: The EU AI Act classes AI used to advertise jobs, filter applications or evaluate candidates as high risk. The 2026 Digital Omnibus moved those obligations to 2 December 2027, but the bans and AI literacy rules already apply, and GDPR Article 22 still governs automated hiring decisions today.
body:
Three dates matter for anyone using AI to hire in the European Union: 2 February 2025, when the AI Act's bans took effect; 2 December 2026, when a second round of transparency and prohibition changes lands; and 2 December 2027, the new date for the high risk rules that cover most recruitment software. The middle and last dates are recent. They come from Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, which was adopted on 8 July 2026, published in the Official Journal on 24 July and in force from 27 July, as summarised in an EY legal alert.

This explainer covers what the AI Act means for recruiters and talent teams after that amendment. It is not legal advice; check your own setup with counsel.

Which recruiting tools count as high risk

Annex III of the AI Act lists employment as a high risk area. The recruitment entry covers AI systems intended to be used for recruiting or selecting people, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates. A second entry covers decisions about promotion, termination, task allocation and monitoring or evaluating workers, as Ogletree lays out.

In practice that reaches resume screeners and ranking engines, AI interview scoring, chat or phone screeners that decide who moves forward, sourcing tools that rank candidates for a role, and ad platforms that choose who sees a job. A scheduling assistant that only books a slot, or a writing aid for job descriptions, is usually outside the list because it does not evaluate people. Our explainer on ATS and AI resume screening shows where screening logic tends to sit inside these tools.

What the Digital Omnibus changed

The original Act applied the Annex III high risk rules from 2 August 2026. The Omnibus postponed them to 2 December 2027, and moved high risk safety components in regulated products, under Annex I, to 2 August 2028. Per EY, it also narrowed the definition of a safety component, softened the AI literacy duty in Article 4 from ensuring a level of literacy to taking measures that promote it, added a legal basis for limited processing of special category data to detect and correct bias, and added two new prohibited practices covering AI that generates non consensual intimate images or child sexual abuse material.

Those new bans, and the Article 50(2) duty to mark AI generated content for systems already on the market before 2 August 2026, apply from 2 December 2026, according to CASRAI's summary of the regulation. For most hiring teams the marking rule falls on vendors of generative tools, not on employers, but it will show up in contract updates this winter.

What already applies today

The delay does not make recruitment AI unregulated in the meantime. The Article 5 bans have applied since 2 February 2025, and one of them targets the workplace directly: emotion recognition in workplaces is prohibited except for medical or safety reasons. A video interview tool that infers enthusiasm or stress from a candidate's face is the obvious risk. Biometric categorisation that infers sensitive traits such as race or political views is also banned.

GDPR also applies in full. Article 22 gives people the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing that significantly affects them, with exceptions for explicit consent, contract necessity and authorisation by law. On 11 November 2026 the European Data Protection Board said its 2027 coordinated enforcement action will review Article 22 compliance and the right of access for automated decision making in employment, including candidate screening tools, as reported by IAPP. Data protection authorities will be asking employers about screening tools well before the AI Act's high risk date.

Provider or deployer: who does what

The Act splits duties between the provider, who builds the system and places it on the market, and the deployer, who uses it. Most employers are deployers. Vendors carry the heavier load: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, accuracy and robustness testing, a conformity assessment, CE marking and registration in the EU database.

From 2 December 2027, an employer deploying a high risk hiring tool must, under Article 26:

  • use it according to the provider's instructions for use
  • assign human oversight to people with the competence, training and authority to override it
  • make sure input data it controls is relevant and sufficiently representative
  • monitor the system and report serious incidents or risks to the provider and authorities
  • keep the logs the system generates for at least six months
  • inform workers' representatives and affected workers before using a high risk system in the workplace
  • tell candidates and employees when a high risk system is used to make or assist decisions about them

Article 86 adds a right for affected people to receive a clear explanation of the role the AI system played in a decision that significantly affects them. An employer that puts its own name on a tool, or substantially modifies it, can become a provider and take on the full set of provider duties.

Who is covered outside the EU

The Act reaches providers that place systems on the EU market wherever they are based, deployers established in the EU, and providers or deployers outside the EU when the system's output is used in the EU. A US company screening applicants for a role in Berlin is in scope for that role. Many global employers will simply apply EU standards to all hiring, which is also how teams have handled the Colorado AI law and New York City's bias audit rule.

Penalties

Using a prohibited practice can cost up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Breaching most other obligations, including deployer duties for high risk systems, can cost up to EUR 15 million or 3%. Smaller companies face the lower of the two amounts.

A 2026 to 2027 plan for talent teams

  1. Inventory every tool that touches candidates and mark which ones filter, rank, score or target. Include features switched on inside your ATS.
  2. Remove or disable anything that infers emotion from video or voice.
  3. Check each automated step against GDPR Article 22 now: is there meaningful human review before a rejection, and can you answer a candidate's access request?
  4. Ask vendors for their AI Act plan: classification, conformity assessment timing, instructions for use and the logs they will expose to you.
  5. Name the people who will provide human oversight and train them; the softer Article 4 duty still expects documented measures.
  6. Draft candidate notices and a works council briefing so they are ready before December 2027.

Teams that already run AI phone screening or automated ranking should start with step three, because that is where enforcement attention is landing first.

faq.q: Is AI used in recruitment high risk under the EU AI Act?
faq.a: Yes, when it is intended to place targeted job ads, analyse and filter applications or evaluate candidates. Those uses are listed in Annex III, so the high risk obligations apply to them.

faq.q: When do the AI Act's high risk rules apply to hiring tools?
faq.a: From 2 December 2027. The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, moved the date from 2 August 2026.

faq.q: Does anything in the AI Act already apply to recruiting?
faq.a: Yes. The Article 5 bans, including emotion recognition in the workplace, have applied since 2 February 2025, and the AI literacy measures in Article 4 apply as well, in the softer form set by the Omnibus.

faq.q: Does the AI Act apply to US employers?
faq.a: It applies when a US employer deploys AI whose output is used in the EU, for example screening applicants for a job based in the EU.

faq.q: What does GDPR Article 22 mean for AI screening?
faq.a: Candidates have the right not to be rejected by a solely automated decision unless an exception such as explicit consent applies, so meaningful human review before a rejection is the safest default.

faq.q: What are the fines for breaking the AI Act in hiring?
faq.a: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices, and up to EUR 15 million or 3% for most other breaches, including deployer obligations.

title: Will AI replace recruiters? What changes, what stays human, and how to adapt
description: Will AI replace recruiters? A 2026 look at which recruiting tasks AI already handles, which still need people, what Gartner analysts told TA leaders in October, and how recruiters can adapt.
short: No, not as a profession, but AI is replacing large parts of the recruiter's task list. Sourcing, screening for clear criteria, outreach drafting and scheduling are moving to software. Judgment about fit, hiring manager advice, closing offers and fairness oversight remain human work, and they are becoming most of the job.
body:
The honest answer splits in two. AI is not on track to remove the recruiter role, but it is removing chunks of what recruiters spend their days on, and it is doing so faster than most job descriptions are being rewritten. A recruiter whose week is mostly keyword searches, copy and paste messages and calendar juggling is doing work that software now does. A recruiter whose week is mostly advising hiring managers, assessing people and closing candidates is doing work that is getting more valuable, not less.

What AI already does in recruiting

Most of the tasks below were manual a few years ago and are now routine features in recruiting software:

  • Sourcing. AI search reads a role description and returns matching profiles, rather than waiting for a recruiter to build Boolean strings.
  • Screening against clear criteria. Tools rank applications against must have requirements and flag gaps.
  • Outreach drafting and sequencing. Personalized first messages and follow ups are written and sent on a schedule.
  • Scheduling. Interview times are matched across calendars without a coordinator in the loop.
  • Notes and summaries. Interview transcripts become structured scorecards in minutes.

Some products now chain these steps into one agent. Noon, for example, sources candidates against a role brief and runs email and SMS outreach for recruiting teams until a reply turns into a booked call. Tools like this change the unit of work from a single search or message to a whole funnel stage.

What the analysts said in October 2026

At the Gartner HR Symposium/Xpo on 26 October 2026, senior director analyst Jamie Kohn described the pressure clearly, as reported by HR Dive. Application volume has more than doubled in the last two years. The old firewall that kept AI out of candidate screening and assessment is crumbling, and recruiters will use AI whether employers approve it or not. Kohn also said keeping AI permanently out of screening is not sustainable, and that roles that are stable and repeatable, with clear criteria and high scale, are the lower risk place to accelerate it.

Her other point matters more for the replacement question. Recruiters are asked to act strategically, yet the system around them rewards speed and deference to hiring managers on open roles only. Her fix was to measure what employers actually want from recruiters, such as slate quality, time to productivity and candidate confidence. None of those metrics is something a sourcing tool can own on its own.

What stays human

Four parts of recruiting resist automation, and they are the parts hiring managers notice most:

  • Defining the role. Turning a vague request into a brief with real must haves takes a conversation and some pushback.
  • Judging ambiguous fit. When skills are hard to observe or success is hard to define, AI evaluation becomes risky, a point Kohn made directly.
  • Closing. Counteroffers, relocation, family timing and compensation tradeoffs are negotiated person to person.
  • Accountability. Laws such as the Colorado AI Act and the EU AI Act expect humans to oversee automated hiring decisions and answer for them.

Which recruiting jobs are most exposed

Exposure follows the task mix. Sourcer roles built around list building, coordinator roles built around scheduling, and high volume screening desks for repeatable hourly roles will shrink or merge as agents absorb their core tasks. Full cycle recruiters, executive search consultants and agency recruiters who own client relationships are less exposed, because their value sits in judgment and trust. Expect fewer people per requisition rather than no people.

How recruiters can adapt

  • Learn to brief and audit AI tools: write precise criteria, review a sample of rejected candidates and correct the scoring.
  • Move time from searching to advising: bring hiring managers market data, slate comparisons and clear tradeoffs.
  • Own the candidate experience in a world where many applications are AI assisted; verify identity and skills early.
  • Track the metrics Kohn named, such as slate quality and time to productivity, so your impact is visible beyond time to fill.

For a deeper look at how these systems actually make decisions, see our explainers on ATS and AI resume screening and on the AI recruiting assistant.

faq.q: Will AI replace recruiters completely?
faq.a: No. AI is taking over sourcing, screening against clear criteria, outreach drafting and scheduling, but role definition, judging ambiguous fit, closing offers and accountability for hiring decisions remain human work.

faq.q: Which recruiting jobs are most at risk from AI?
faq.a: Roles built mainly around list building, interview scheduling or screening high volumes of applicants for repeatable roles are the most exposed. Full cycle, executive search and client facing agency recruiters are less exposed.

faq.q: How is AI changing recruiting in 2026?
faq.a: Application volume has more than doubled in two years according to a Gartner analyst, and employers are moving AI into screening and assessment, starting with stable, repeatable roles that have clear criteria.

faq.q: What skills do recruiters need to work alongside AI?
faq.a: Writing precise role criteria, auditing AI recommendations, advising hiring managers with market data, verifying candidate identity and skills, and closing offers.

faq.q: Is it still worth becoming a recruiter?
faq.a: Yes, if you build the advisory and judgment side of the job. The task mix is shifting away from manual searching and toward assessment, influence and closing.
